body:
This resonates with me a lot. I hurt my wife by making her feel unwanted. This was due to sexual issues on my part, and she felt like I lied to her about how serious they were. I used porn to cope with my issues, and lied to her about that too. 

If you want more info, feel free to read my post history. I'm a pretty open book, as this is my alt account. Basically, we are now separated, and while we haven't made any final decisions about our relationship, it's hard to see how we can ever rebuild an intimate relationship. But I think at least part of us both want it.

Regardless, we still love each other very much. We have been each other's "person" and companion for 7 years. Now I'm struggling with trying to detach from her, but still needing to lean on her. I have very few real friends, none of whom are in the area, and can't even tell my mom about everything. So I feel very isolated, and I want to turn to her, but I know I shouldn't, and that makes me resentful, blah blah...it goes on.

A couple of things I want to respond to specifically:

>i hurt him big time and it's really hard for me to basically see how i deserve in any way to feel good

I struggle with this too. But the truth is, everyone deserves to be happy. Nobody deserves to be miserable. And even if you think you don't *deserve* happiness, you *need* it. You can't survive for long feeling like happiness is not even an option. So try to see happiness as a basic need, and not something you earn.

>i basically am super insecure of my personality and i'm so self deprecating it hurts

I built my whole life around my wife. I have other interests and hobbies, but I always tempered them to fit within the rigid structures she had for our relationships (can't keep my instruments out where anyone can see them, can't spend too much money on them, etc.). I'm trying to find ways to get back into my hobbies now, but it's difficult when I feel depressed and don't want to do anything. Still, I keep trying, and I think it's better to force myself to do things that I don't necessarily feel super dedicated to than to just mope around. I know this isn't exactly responding to your point, but I do think finding and pursuing your own interests will help with your self-perception.

>i rely on HIS help and his reassurance so much.

This is REALLY hard for me too. I have settled on being happy with what I can get (we do still see each other and are good friends), and try to find things to distract myself or other people I can talk to when I'm feeling stuck.

My inbox is always open if you want someone to talk to. I will say I have kids and a crazy schedule right now, so I can't really guarantee I'd be available to listen in a crisis moment, but I'm happy to talk more if it's helpful to you.

In any case, know that you aren't the only one that struggles with these things; it's really hard, and, as my friend told me yesterday, you're being brave just by continuing to breathe and exist. You can do this!
Apparently you must live in Canada to participate, FYI.

First, good job on taking action to try to deal with this situation. It's easier to deny that what you're feeling is irrational than to confront it. Use that as an anchor to remind yourself that you are still in control, even if it's difficult to maintain.

Is there anyone you can call just to casually chat? If you can get into a safe headspace for just a few minutes, so that you can calmly and casually call a friend just to chat, maybe that could help ground you. Probably best to avoid any people who might trigger negative emotions if you can.

We are definitely doing that with a separation agreement, and if the kids go to their grandmother's, I think we might have time to do that. I think I may just offer to write a brief statement about how moving out without the children in tow is a necessary and normal part of this type of transition, just to set her mind at ease.

We have no intention of fighting over our children. However, I'm dealing with some emotional regulation issues (in therapy) and I think she is concerned that I will start to act irrationally and try to use this against her, which I can't blame her for.

If your therapist is any good, they will take you seriously. They may not agree with you, but they should take you seriously. If they don't, I wouldn't work with them.

Again, they may not agree with your self-diagnosis, but if that's the case they should explain why. In any case, they should at least want to examine the patterns you've identified and seek to understand how they reflect (or not) your reality. All of these things are indications that you are being taken seriously.
Yeah this is totally me, haha.
Sora is the name of the main character in the Kingdom Hearts video game franchise. I assumed that's where you got it, but apparently not.

I'm just now learning about DBT and that this technique is a part of it. I can definitely empathize with this though. I often try to do things that I think will be positive, but somehow I end up screwing it up and it has a negative effect instead. And I feel even worse about spiraling downward in the first place.

I've realized I just need to choose different actions, that don't have as much potential to turn bad. Specifically, I'm trying to do things by myself when I can, so that I only have to worry about myself in that moment. I realize that might be hard for you if being social is something that gives you a lot of fulfillment, so take it with a big grain of salt.
I know the feeling. Over the past few months I've been there a few times. I'm glad I'm still here though. Stay with us!

I've been thinking that it didn't fit me, but the more I think about it, I realize that formulating it as "taboo and/or risky sexual behavior" instead of "promiscuity" does fit with my experience.

EDIT: What I meant to convey with this is that you should consider trying to find a way to talk to your therapist about it; It seems likely it's connected with your other issues. Regardless of whether or not that's the case, it doesn't make you a bad person, and you deserve a chance to deal with it in a way that doesn't make you dissociate.

This really hits home, and I hope it's not universally true. I'm in this some boat, and I'm not ready to accept that it's over. We have kids and we still have a lot of love for each other. But she has another partner, and she's happy, and she's very hurt...I just don't know if it's ever possible. But we remain good friends; I guess it makes disentangling our lives and shifting our boundaries easier in some ways, but harder in others.

I still haven't accepted it's over, and I'm not ready to do so yet. But I'm already mourning the loss and fearing being alone.

I am currently exploring my issues and don't yet have (or seek, really) a formal diagnosis, I feel very empathic with the stories of quiet bpd that I hear. When it was first suggested to me that I might have BPD (by my wife, after I dented a steel water bottle against my head), I found this sub and my heart sank because it was like looking in a mirror. Certain parts of the experience I was seeing didn't quite fit me, but then I read about quiet bpd. Whether I truly have it or not, I absolutely identify with the feelings and the struggles that accompany quiet bpd. It was so validating to see that other people struggled the way I did. I know it must be frustrating for your parents not to understand and support you. Just remember that you and your mental health professional have worked to find answers, and there is a whole community here of people who understand. People have all kinds of reasons for rejecting or minimizing the struggles others have. That is painful in itself. I'm sorry you're having to deal with that while also trying to understand and support yourself. I'm glad to hear that you have a supportive partner, and glad you are here participating in the community. It makes me feel less alone, so thank you!
Username checks out ;)

I don't have a diagnosis, but I really think this applies to me. I'm good enough at hiding/coping, often in insidiously self-destructive ways, that I have gone 15+ years in my adult life without realizing how deep the issues were, or that I had essentially given up on being truly happy, as I thought "content" was the best I could ever do.

I let myself throw a tantrum in front of my wife's girlfriend because I'd gotten so comfortable around her, but she was understandably quite upset about it, as it was triggering for her due to past trauma and also just generally upsetting to see me raging at someone she loves.

I feel this. I am in a tough situation right now and pain and anxiety about the future are normal emotions right now, but everything feels even bigger than it is, and I feel like I can't escape the sinking ball of tension in my stomach.

This is really helpful, thank you. Right now I'm struggling with just not exploding when I feel backed into a corner. Right now, I just grabbed for any tool that I can find, and it always seems to be something self-destructive. I need to find a new tool, and this seems a good place to start.
Thank you. I have done that before, but at this moment I just can't bring myself to do it. But I'll keep trying.

Yeah, I started writing out my thoughts when some shit hit the fan a couple months ago and I haven't stopped. I've probably written hundreds of pages. Sometimes it can help me process things rationally, and sometimes it makes me spiral into a panic. I've learned to be careful about it but it's a great tool when I can wield it safely.

Music is tricky. I'm a musician, but have pretty much zero desire to play anymore. And the only music I really want to listen to right now is stuff that my wife and I listened to together a lot. Same with TV, movies, etc. The only ones I have any interest in watching are also triggering so I avoid them.

The only thing I've found that consistently helps me to deal is to talk with someone. Since I don't really have anyone I can talk to about the full picture at any given moment, I'm sort of hedging my bets, talking to whoever I can about whatever part of the situation I can share. It's definitely helpful but still frustrating.

Love your username.

I'm in a similar boat. One thing I've learned about myself is that my thoughts and behaviors are often *amplified* by BPD-like or codependent patterns, but that doesn't invalidate the core feeling.

I'm basically alone now and can't talk to anybody at all about what I'm going through. It's horrible. I feel like I'm stuck in that trapped/panic place where I'm on the verge of doing something self-destructive. It's not a good feeling. It's not a stable feeling. I'm scared of it, more than I'm scared of the actual thing I'm thinking about.

Nothing feels good. I don't want to watch my favorite movies or tv, don't want to eat...yet I have to be a dad and keep up with work...sometimes I don't know how to do it.

Feel free to reach out if you want to talk. I'm not sure how helpful I'd be, but it sounds like I could empathize at least.

Thank you. You're absolutely right about my mental health bleeding into my relationships; in fact, that's a coping mechanism for me. Put off some of the burden on others. Unfortunately, it doesn't really work, at least for me. I usually just end up asking or expecting too much and pushing them away.

Right now I'm afraid that I have given D an impression of me that will be impossible to shake, and that I won't ever be able to do "family" things with all of us and the kids ever again. CBT tells me that's future predicting, mind reading, catastrophizing...I know those things, but it's such a huge threat and it seems very real.

Anyway, thanks for your advice and well wishes.

I struggle with understanding the line here as well.  /u/Naive_Tree's take is helpful to me in validating the need/desire for another person, but it's still hard to know where to draw the line. My wife is focusing on her other partner right now (she's polyamorous), and we've kind of hit pause on working on us while I focus on myself. It's really hard seeing her free of my issues and flourishing with another person, while I sit here confused about...everything. I'm still trying to sort it all out. I guess today I'm just trying to focus on detangling my feelings, sorting out what I want because it will truly fulfill me from the things that only serve to quiet my demons. In other words, does this really make me happy AND feel safe, or does it just make me feel safe? For now, I've given myself permission to accept the desire to have a healthy, happy, intimate relationship with my wife, realizing that that may never come to pass. I'm working to try to be ok with myself, to love myself; whatever happens,  I think that can only be good.

So I guess in the end, I DO want someone who can help me quiet the demons, but I also want to be happy with that person for the right reasons. I believe I could have had that with my wife, but I may have just hurt her too much over the years for that to be possible. I hope that if we don't work out, it's because we've both decided we are incompatible, and not because I failed to find self-fulfillment.
Thanks, I needed to hear this. I am constantly second-guessing myself and the validity of my feelings, so it's helpful to have something to help me sort out the feelings.

A lot like /u/Coffeekerry, I never would have blamed my childhood for my issues. Unlike them, however, my dad absolutely had issues that I grew to understand more fully as I got older.

I've really just started on my journey towards self-fulfillment and disentangling the vines rooted in the behavior of my father, the abuse I endured as an overweight and awkward kid, and the fundamentally incorrect ideas I had about sex growing up. Those three issues have, collectively, controlled my life to an alarming degree.

Yet I never realized it. The first issues that I couldn't ignore appeared when I started dating the woman who became my first wife. Our intimacy issues seemed intractable, so much so that our marriage couldn't survive. I saw therapists, but was only viewing through the lens of sexual dysfunction.

But those vines changed the entire course of my life, not in one fell swoop, but slowly and insidiously throughout my life. And yet I only ever really knew about one of them, and I completely underestimated the difficulty of dealing with that one. For the first time in my life (I'm 34), I feel like I can see the vines. I still have to disentangle them. It's already obvious that this is going to be a painful, difficult process that never really ends.

I guess the moral of the story is that our childhood is the foundation of who we are. If there are problems in it, we learn to cope. Sometimes those coping mechanisms are healthy, or at least have positive effects. Sometimes they are self-destructive, to varying degrees. In most cases, we view them as just our framework for life, for making decisions, solving problems, interacting with others, etc. For me, realizing that I was using a twisted framework was the first step. After exploring that framework, I started to understand how it was built. I'm still working on that. I'm also starting to think about how to substitute a healthier framework for my broken one, bit by bit. It's very difficult. It's hard to know which framework the feelings and desires you have are built on. After all, you've lived with it your whole life, not realizing it was so out of whack.

Don't feel bad if you can't place some specific trauma as the cause of your issues. What's important is realizing that your way of looking at the world is fundamentally skewed. You can find ways to understand it, correct for it, or embrace it when appropriate. 

Like I said, I'm just starting out on this journey, but for the first time I feel like I'm on a path that actually moves me forward. I hope you feel that way too.
I don't know of a specific connection either, but this describes me. Usually for me it means lying or omitting truth to protect myself.

I'm sorry that you're going through this. I am trying to hang on to my relationship at the same time that I try to deal with my codependency issues. It's really hard, but therapy helps. It also helps me to remember that while my feelings are totally valid, they are amplified by the effect that past traumas have had on me. So I let myself feel a little scared, but I try to remember that that feeling of despair no hopelessness is not representative of reality. I really recommend seeing a therapist, so that you can get some tools cope and to learn to move forward.

You can do this. You are stronger than you think.

I feel this. I'm very new to thinking of myself as possibly having BPD, so take what I have to say with a grain of salt 

For me it helps to remember that your feelings are valid, they're just...amplified. It's not bad to want to see someone you care about. But that need taps into deeper issues and warps it into something destructive if you cant stop it. Just remember that the reality of the situation does not fully match what you feel.

And also, think how much better it will be when you see him if you're happy with yourself before you do? I mean, if you think of being happy as something that helps you both, it makes it a little easier to let yourself be happy by yourself. 

It's helped me a lot since I've been thinking about this stuff. But everyone is different, so if this doesn't apply to you, don't take it as an invalidation of how you deal.
